_about: LanWatch router knowledge base: (1) 'checks' is the router hardening checklist shown on the Advice page; (2) 'brands' says how to find each check on common router brands. A brand is recognised from the router's MAC maker (vendor_match, lower-case pieces of the maker name) or its name (name_match). Menu names change between models and software versions, so every 'where' hint is a starting point, not a promise. ADVICE ONLY: LanWatch never logs in to the router or changes it. Used by app/services/router_advice.py.

admin_password.title: Change the router's admin password
admin_password.why: The router's settings page controls your whole network and can be opened from every device at home. Factory passwords (often 'admin' or the one on the sticker) are widely known.
steps: Open the router's settings page or app (see 'How to open it' above).
Find 'Administrator', 'Admin password', 'Management' or 'System > Password'.
Choose a long password you don't use anywhere else and save it somewhere safe, such as a password manager.
This is NOT your Wi-Fi password: it only protects the settings page.

firmware.title: Keep the router's software (firmware) up to date
firmware.why: Router makers fix security holes through firmware updates. An out-of-date router is one of the most common ways home networks are attacked.
steps: Open the router's settings page or app and find 'Firmware', 'Software update', 'Update' or 'System Tools'.
Check for an update and install it. Don't switch the router off while it updates.
Turn on automatic updates if the router offers them.
If your internet provider supplied the router, it usually updates it for you. If the router is more than about 5 years old and gets no more updates, ask your provider about a replacement.

wifi_security.title: Use WPA2 or WPA3 and a strong Wi-Fi password
wifi_security.why: Older Wi-Fi security (WEP, WPA, or 'Open') can be broken in minutes. A short Wi-Fi password can be guessed by anyone within range of your house.
steps: Open the router's Wi-Fi or Wireless settings.
Set the security to 'WPA3', 'WPA2/WPA3' or 'WPA2-PSK (AES)'. Never 'Open', 'WEP' or 'WPA' on its own.
Use a Wi-Fi password of at least 12 characters (a few random words work well).
If you change the password, every device will need the new one, so do it when you have time to reconnect them.

wps.title: Turn off WPS (the push-button / PIN connection)
wps.why: WPS lets devices join without the Wi-Fi password. Its PIN method in particular has well-known weaknesses that let attackers get in.
steps: Open the router's Wi-Fi or Wireless settings and look for 'WPS'.
Switch WPS off (or at least the 'PIN' method).
You can still connect new devices by typing the Wi-Fi password.

upnp.title: Turn off UPnP if you don't need it
upnp.why: UPnP lets any device at home open doors (ports) through your router to the internet without asking. Malware on one device can use it to expose others.
steps: Open the router's settings and look for 'UPnP' (often under 'Advanced', 'NAT', 'Network' or 'Home network').
Switch it off.
If an online game or video call stops working afterwards, you can switch it back on: it's a trade-off between convenience and safety.

remote_management.title: Turn off remote management from the internet
remote_management.why: Remote management lets the router's settings page be opened from anywhere on the internet, where attackers constantly try passwords.
steps: Open the router's settings and look for 'Remote management', 'Remote access', 'Web access from WAN' or 'Access control'.
Switch it off, unless you really need to change router settings while away from home.
Internet providers sometimes keep their own remote access for support (often called TR-069). That's normal and usually can't be switched off.

guest_network.title: Use a guest network for visitors and smart gadgets
guest_network.why: Devices on the guest network can use the internet but can't see your computers and phones, so a visitor's infected phone or a poorly secured smart plug can't reach them.
steps: Open the router's Wi-Fi settings and look for 'Guest network' or 'Guest Wi-Fi'.
Switch it on with its own password, and make sure 'Allow guests to see each other / access the local network' is off.
Give that password to visitors, and connect smart-home gadgets (plugs, bulbs, TVs) to it if they still work there.

port_forwarding.title: Review port forwarding rules
port_forwarding.why: Each port forwarding rule makes a device at home reachable from the whole internet. Old rules for games, cameras or servers you no longer use are open doors.
steps: Open the router's settings and look for 'Port forwarding', 'Virtual servers', 'NAT' or 'Applications'.
Delete any rule you don't recognise or no longer need.
Also check for 'DMZ' and make sure it is off: it forwards everything to one device.

arcadyan.name: Arcadyan
arcadyan.open: Supplied by internet providers (in NZ, the Spark Smart Modem). Type the address on its label, usually http://192.168.1.254, into a web browser.

huawei.name: Huawei
huawei.open: Usually supplied by an internet provider. Type the address on its label (often http://192.168.1.254 or http://192.168.1.1) into a web browser.

tp_link.name: TP-Link
tp_link.open: Home models: http://tplinkwifi.net or http://192.168.0.1 in a web browser, or the TP-Link Tether app. Deco mesh: the Deco app. Provider-supplied models (e.g. 2degrees, Contact) may use the Aginet or TP-Link app instead.

where.firmware: On most Archer models: Advanced > System Tools > Firmware Upgrade (or System > Firmware Update). Deco: More > Update Deco.
where.upnp: On most Archer models: Advanced > NAT Forwarding > UPnP. Deco: More > Advanced > UPnP.
where.wps: On most Archer models: Advanced > Wireless > WPS.
where.remote_management: On most Archer models: Advanced > System Tools > Administration > Remote Management.
where.port_forwarding: On most Archer models: Advanced > NAT Forwarding > Virtual Servers.

netcomm.name: NetComm
netcomm.open: Supplied by NZ providers such as Slingshot, Orcon and Contact. Type the address on its label into a web browser (Contact's NF18ACV uses http://192.168.20.1).

where.admin_password: NetComm modems have several logins (for example 'admin' and 'support'). Change the passwords of both 'admin' and 'support'; Slingshot recommends leaving the others alone.

nokia.name: Nokia
nokia.open: Most settings are in the Nokia WiFi app. The web page's 'admin' password is on the sticker underneath the modem.

where.admin_password: In the web page: Maintenance > Password (on FastMile 5G models).

avm.name: AVM FRITZ!Box
avm.open: Type http://fritz.box into a web browser. The FRITZ!Box password is on the label underneath.

where.firmware: System > Update (you can also switch on automatic updates there).
where.upnp: Home Network > Network > Network Settings: untick 'Permit access for applications' / 'Transmit status information over UPnP'.
where.remote_management: Internet > Permit Access (or MyFRITZ!): make sure internet access to the FRITZ!Box is off.

netgear.name: NETGEAR
netgear.open: Type http://routerlogin.net into a web browser, or use the Nighthawk (or Orbi) app.

where.firmware: ADVANCED > Administration > Router Update (or Firmware Update).
where.port_forwarding: ADVANCED > Advanced Setup > Port Forwarding / Port Triggering.

asus.name: ASUS
asus.open: Type http://router.asus.com into a web browser, or use the ASUS Router app.

where.remote_management: Administration > System > Enable Web Access from WAN (set to No).

d_link.name: D-Link
d_link.open: Usually http://192.168.0.1 in a web browser, or the D-Link app (AQUILA PRO models).

linksys.name: Linksys
linksys.open: Type http://myrouter.local into a web browser, or use the Linksys app.

google.name: Google Nest Wifi
google.open: Managed only through the Google Home app. Its software updates automatically.

where.admin_password: There's no separate admin password: the router is protected by your Google account, so use a strong password and 2-step verification on it.
where.firmware: Updates are automatic; nothing to do.

eero.name: eero
eero.open: Managed only through the eero app. Its software updates automatically.

where.admin_password: There's no separate admin password: the router is protected by your eero (Amazon) account, so use a strong password and 2-step verification on it.
where.firmware: Updates are automatic; check the update time in the eero app under Settings > Software updates.

ubiquiti.name: Ubiquiti UniFi
ubiquiti.open: Managed through the UniFi Network app or its web console.

technicolor.name: Technicolor / Vantiva
technicolor.open: Usually supplied by an internet provider. Type the address on its label (often http://192.168.1.1) into a web browser.

sagemcom.name: Sagemcom
sagemcom.open: Usually supplied by an internet provider. Type the address on its label into a web browser.

zte.name: ZTE
zte.open: Usually supplied by an internet provider. Type the address on its label into a web browser.
